question: What is the meaning of primary energy intensity (pei) in relation to material layers, materials?
description: Primary Energy Intensity (PEI) in relation to material layers and materials refers to the amount of primary energy required to produce one kilogram of a material. It is expressed in megajoules per kilogram (MJ/kg). PEI is an important indicator in life cycle assessment (LCA) as it helps to evaluate the energy consumption and environmental impact associated with the production of materials. In the context of the MP-assessment method, PEI is used to assess the environmental impact of different material layers within a building component, considering the energy required to produce each material layer. This information is crucial for generating an information-rich BIM-based MP, which aims to assess the recycling potential and environmental impact of a building. The PEI values for different materials are obtained from the IBO-database, and the material layers' thicknesses and volumes are obtained from the BIM-model. The PEI values are then used to calculate the environmental impact of each material layer, considering the energy consumption and emissions associated with the production of the materials. This information is used to generate an MP-assessment method, which aims to assess the recycling potential and environmental impact of a building. 3.2. MP-model 
The MP-model - the material informed BIM-model - is generated 
based on the initial BIM-model from the point cloud, as well as the data 
of both material assessment approaches. The BIM-model was generated 
manually, including all building components (walls, suspended ceilings, 
roof, foundation, windows and doors) and their accurate geometry, but 
without material information. Based on the material assessments DA and 
UMA, multi-layered elements, with the exact material composition and 
thickness of each layer were generated in BIM. 
As a result, a BIM-model consisting of all relevant material infor­
mation and accurate geometry of the use case for follow-up generation 
of the MP was generated. A list of all elements including the material 
names, thickness and areas was exported from BIM and was used for 
mapping the relevant eco-indicators from IBO eco-inventory. 
4. Results 
For generating the MP, the density and other relevant indicators, as 
described in section 2.1, were obtained from IBO and mapped to each 
material layer. The quality was obtained from the results of the DA, 
based on which the recycling grade from IBO was adapted. The com­
ponents with the largest mass according to the UMA and the largest area 
according to the BIM-model were considered for demonstrating the 
application of the MP on the existing building. The foundation repre­
sents ~72% of the mass of the total building (1059 t out of 1456 t in 
total), as Fig. 6 shows. The exterior walls have a total area of ~814 m2. 
Accordingly, the foundation and the exterior walls were assessed. The 
input parameters are shown in Tables 2 and 3 for the exterior walls as 
well as in Tables 6 and 7 for the foundation. Tables 4 and 5 consist of the 
exterior walls results, whereby Tables 8 and 9 of the foundations results. 
4.1. MP-assessment results of the exterior walls 
The exterior walls comprise of three layers – the trapezoidal sheet out 
of steel, the mineral wool and aerated concrete. Due to the trapezoidal 
shape of the steel cladding the total area was assessed separately and 
leads to a larger area than the exterior walls are in reality. As aerated 
concrete is the load-bearing material, it is the thickest layer. The high 
density of aerated concrete, as shown in Table 3, leads to a large mass 
(~163 t out of ~176 t in total) and makes it the material with the highest 
influence on the results. The recycling potential of the exterior walls is 
~52% (~91 t of recyclable mass and ~85 t of waste mass). Apart from 
concrete, the steel sheet has a large impact on the total GWP and PEI of 
the exterior walls. The significantly large amount of GWP and PEI in case 
of steel are mainly due to the high input parameters of GWP and PEI for 
steel, as displayed in Table 3. In Table 4 the share of recycling and waste 
at the end-of-life stage is displayed, whereby aerated concrete has the 
largest share in both. Even though the mass of the steel sheet is less than 
1/10 of the mass of aerated concrete, the results for GWP and PEI are 
very close: 26.448 kgCO2 (steel), 36.937 kgCO2 (aerated concrete) and 
387.410 MJ (steel), 458.870 (aerated concrete), as Table 5 shows. The 
low recycling grade of mineral wool does not have a significant impact 
on the total share of waste, since its mass is not very high. The mineral 
wool originally has the grade 3 (Table 2), but was downgraded to grade 
5, since in practice it is categorized as hazardous waste in Austria, using 
the waste code for asbestos waste, even though it does not contain 
asbestos. Currently, in Austria, mineral wool is seldom recycled, since 
only a few mineral wool manufacturers recycle their own products, 
which was not the case in this use case.

are used for the LCA, namely the Global Warming Potential (GWP), the 
Acidification Potential (AP) and Primary Energy Intensity (PEI), 
expressed in [kgCO2/kg], [kgSO2/kg] and [MJ/kg], respectively. For all 
three indicators, only the manufacturing phase is considered. By linking 
the mass of each material-layer of an element to the grades from 1 to 5, 
as well as to the indicators, the recycling potential and the environ­
mental impact of a building is assessed. 
For generating an MP, information about the material composition 
and geometry is required, which is obtained from the BIM-model. In 
detail, these are all material-layers of a building element (e.g. multi- 
layered wall with concrete, insulation and plaster) with their respec­
tive layer thicknesses and volumes. In order to obtain the mass of a 
material, the density and volume is required. The density is obtained 
from the IBO-database, whereas the volume of a material is obtained 
from the BIM-model. In our previous research, the generation of the 
BIM-based MP was conducted through a bi-directional connection of 
BIM with a material inventory and analysis tool, thus allowing a semi- 
automated workflow. As this is an effortful process, within this paper, 
the semi-automated workflow is not applied. Therefore, the required 
information from the BIM-model is obtained by exporting a spreadsheet 
and mapping the grades from 1 to 5 to the material layers. The main 
obstacle is the acquisition of the required information in order to enable 
the generation of an information rich BIM, since the information about 
the existing building is not sufficient. 
2.2. Adaptation of the MP-assessment method 
The planning documentation on existing buildings is seldom accu­
rate and represents a vague picture of buildings, as previous research has 
shown (Koutamanis et al., 2018; Bergsdal et al., 2007). Lack of infor­
mation represents a great challenge for the efficient compilation of an 
MP. Following information of the assessed building is required for the 
generation of an MP on component level (e.g. walls and slabs): all ma­
terial layers (name of material), thickness, dimensions of the compo­
nent, volume of each material layer (obtained from BIM) and 
separability of material layers. The MP-assessment method does not 
enable a direct integration of separation techniques, as it is based on 
downgrading of material grades. Accordingly, the separability is 
considered as follows: the recycling potential of materials, which are 
difficult to separate from the enclosed layer due to e.g. adhesives used 
for bonding, are downgraded, which means that in such a case a material 
with grade 3 is downgraded to grade 4. Materials which can be sepa­
rated with low effort and do not lead to contamination of the enclosed 
layers, are not downgraded (e.g. screws, nails, dowels). Within this 
paper, the MP-assessment method was applied on a real use case, where 
through destructive methods the separability of materials was analyzed 
on selected building elements as well as documented. As this research is 
based on real data acquired on site, as described in section 2.3, it delivers 
reliable information regarding the separability of materials. As the 
proposed MP-assessment method was initially developed for the build­
ing design stage, as described in 2.1, the quality of the materials did not 
play a crucial role. However, for existing buildings the quality has to be 
integrated in the assessment since at the end-of-life stage the quality of 
material might vary. Accordingly, within the adapted MP, the assigned 
grades from 1 to 5 are downgraded if a material has a lower quality at 
the end-of-life stage.
